item.title: Generative AI in transnational repression cases and the response from AI companies
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Anthropic's September threat intelligence report describes state-linked actors using Claude for surveillance, some of it aimed at dissidents living abroad. In an October commentary for Just Security, Citizen Lab researchers analysed the report and urged AI companies to act on disclosure and notification, detection and refusal, and evidence preservation. Neither document offers settings advice for ordinary users.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 8 sources, including Anthropic, Just Security, Citizen Lab

Anthropic's threat intelligence team published "Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026" on 10 September. Its surveillance chapter lists a series of operations the company found and disrupted between January and July 2026, in which, according to the report, state-linked organisations, contractors working for states and commercial spyware vendors used Claude to build and run surveillance. The report classifies some of these cases as transnational repression aimed at dissidents and diaspora communities living abroad.

Three Citizen Lab researchers analysed the report in a commentary published by Just Security on 12 October, and Citizen Lab's website republished a summary on 22 October. Every case the commentary discusses comes from Anthropic's report. Both documents deal with how attackers use AI services, and neither offers settings advice for ordinary users.

The researchers cite Freedom House's definition, under which digital transnational repression is the use of digital technology by governments to intimidate and silence dissidents in exile and in diaspora communities. Their earlier interview research with affected people found that such threats cause fear and isolation, and lead people to self-censor and withdraw from advocacy.

The researchers group the report's cases into four shifts. The first is cost: digital repression used to depend on language skills, trained intelligence analysts and software engineers, and the researchers read the cases as showing that AI can replace part of that. The second is the processing of open information, since diaspora communities leave large amounts of data on social media, messaging apps, public databases and organisational websites. An AI assistant can compile that scattered data into intelligence reports used to reconstruct personal networks, infer political leanings and locate people, and even to flag their vulnerabilities.

The third shift is building models into fixed workflows, so that a handful of staff can oversee repeated, partly automated surveillance reporting; in one case the system automatically reviewed 15 to 30 or more foreign media articles a day. Fourth, surveillance output can support physical surveillance, coercion, the recruitment of informants and the disruption of civil society groups' work. The researchers also note that the report does not show this reconnaissance led to physical attacks.

According to the report's cases, the model was also used to translate and write messages in dialect, generate multilingual posts for fake online personas, and write code for surveillance tools such as browser extensions. One operation was still at a trial stage and had more than 255 synthetic social media accounts ready, which the report takes as a sign that the accounts were prepared in advance for later use. Unlike the follow-on surveillance described in an earlier news investigation, the report found no evidence that these accounts had been used against real targets before Anthropic banned them. Another operation planned mass reporting and bot amplification against journalists at an exile media outlet, and the report describes this as a plan rather than something carried out.

According to the report, in the same operation that planned mass reporting against the exile journalists, Claude refused several requests for covert interrogation and for generating fake personas at scale. In a case the commentary classifies as domestic surveillance, Claude first refused to produce a surveillance report, but after the request was rephrased the model still produced guidance naming 10 civilians. In another domestic case the commentary mentions, the surveillance system ran entirely on a local model, and Anthropic banned the account but could not disable the system already deployed.

Anthropic's usage policy prohibits using Claude for non-consensual surveillance and profiling, and for violating individuals' civil liberties and human rights. According to the report, the related accounts were banned in every case, and the company improved its ability to detect similar techniques. Where an operation's impact extended beyond the platform, Anthropic shared identifiers and intelligence with industry partners and authorities as appropriate. The report also mentions that some actors used VPNs to get around Anthropic's regional restrictions.

The researchers write that the report reflects only what one company could see and detect over a short period, and that confidence in some attributions is limited. In one case in the report, the actor is assessed only with low confidence to be a contractor working for a state security agency rather than the agency itself.

Perspective

The researchers note that earlier warnings about AI in transnational repression mostly extrapolated from technical capability and had few concrete cases behind them, and they regard Anthropic's report as offering rare operational detail. They suggest that detection should not rely on easily recognised repression keywords, and should instead flag the combination of social media monitoring, geolocation, vulnerability profiling and inference of political leanings, since together these capabilities can point to a transnational repression workflow.

The researchers base their recommendations on the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs), which require companies to address adverse human rights impacts they are involved in. The commentary argues that AI companies should treat transnational repression as a threat category of its own, separate from domestic surveillance and influence operations, and act in three areas. As of 8 November, we found no public response to the commentary from Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind or xAI. On the companies' side, the only document available is Anthropic's September report, which predates the commentary and is not a response to its recommendations.

On the first area, disclosure and notification, Anthropic's report is itself a public disclosure, and its account of the response says information is shared with industry partners and authorities as appropriate. The researchers credit the report's detail and consider that OpenAI, DeepMind and xAI may encounter similar operations, though without standardised reporting there is nothing to assess. They also recommend notifying affected communities, and point out that Google and Apple already have processes for notifying the targets of state-backed attacks. Those notifications go to the companies' own users, whereas the people targeted through an AI service are not necessarily its users, so the researchers recommend community-level notification in formats and languages the recipients can understand.

On the second area, detection and refusal, the researchers credit Anthropic with repeatedly finding and stopping operations before large-scale deployment, while noting that in some cases a rephrased request got around a refusal. Anthropic's report describes improving detection of similar techniques in each case and feeding the investigation findings into its safeguards.

On the third area, evidence preservation, the researchers note that civil lawsuits and criminal investigations have already arisen from cases where digital transnational repression escalated into physical harm. They therefore argue that companies should keep detailed incident records, including attribution data, for future investigations. They also write that what should be kept depends on local law and remains contested.

Neither the commentary nor the Citizen Lab page offers practical advice for people who are targeted. Google and Apple each have processes for notifying the targets of state-backed operations, and the commentary treats them as a reference for AI companies setting up notification of their own.

We, a community based in Taiwan, compared these recommendations with the Asian rules on AI and online platforms we have checked, and the closest parallel to regular public reporting is in Japan. The Act Partially Amending the Public Offices Election Act and the Act on Responses to Infringement of Rights Caused by Distribution of Information through Specified Telecommunications (Act No. 58 of 2026), promulgated on 17 July 2026 and taking effect on 1 March 2027, requires large-scale specified telecommunications service providers to take measures against information that may harm the fairness of elections, under guidelines set by the Minister for Internal Affairs and Communications, and to publish how they implemented those measures each year. That duty is aimed at large platforms and election-related information and does not mention surveillance. South Korea's Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Creation of a Foundation for Trust (the AI Basic Act), which took full effect on 22 January 2026 with a grace period of at least one year for penalties under its transparency provision, requires generative AI providers to label their output (Article 31), which concerns disclosure to users rather than what a provider does when its tools are misused.

Mainland China already places a record-keeping duty on providers, with a different recipient. Under the Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis of Internet Information Services (Order No. 12), issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Ministry of Public Security and in force since 10 January 2023, a provider of deep synthesis services within mainland China that finds its service used to produce or spread false information must take rebuttal measures, keep the relevant records and report to the cyberspace authorities and other competent authorities (Article 11). The researchers want records kept for civil lawsuits and criminal investigations arising from harm to targeted people, whereas the Chinese rule names the cyberspace authorities as the recipient, and the duty is triggered by false information rather than by surveillance.

When reading other AI companies' threat reports, a few things are worth comparing: whether transnational repression is classified separately, what steps the response includes (banning accounts, improving detection, sharing intelligence), whether targeted communities are notified, and what records are kept. Another set of questions concerns effectiveness, since the researchers point out that some refusals were bypassed by rephrasing. When a system runs on a local model, banning the account does not stop it, so how early detection needs to happen to be useful is also worth comparing. The researchers note that the industry has no standardised reporting, and whether companies can be compared will depend on whether a common format is established.

item.title: Privacy Badger for Safari on macOS
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: On 19 October, EFF released a Safari version of Privacy Badger, its tracker-blocking browser extension. It runs only on the Mac and requires Safari 26.5 and macOS 15.7.7 or later. As of 8 November, there is no Safari version for iPhone or iPad.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 18 sources, including EFF, Apple, GitHub

The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), a US digital rights group, released a Safari version of Privacy Badger on 19 October. Privacy Badger is a free browser extension developed by EFF that automatically learns to recognise and block trackers. The Safari version supports only the Mac and needs Safari 26.5 or later, and the system requirement listed on its Mac App Store page is macOS 15.7.7 or later. As of 8 November, it cannot be installed in Safari on iPhone or iPad.

According to EFF's announcement, Privacy Badger already has more than 4 million users. In the press release, EFF's technical staff mention that Safari support has long been one of the most frequent requests from users. The announcement credits improvements in Safari's extension support for making a release possible for Safari 26.5 and later.

According to the announcement, Safari's default browsing mode limits the information trackers can access but still lets them load. Privacy Badger stops trackers from loading in the first place, so it can block tracking techniques that get around Safari's protections. Widgets such as embedded tweets, comment sections and video players can share data even if the user never clicks them, and Privacy Badger replaces them with placeholders that load only when clicked.

Privacy Badger also automatically sends the Global Privacy Control (GPC) signal, which tells websites not to sell or share the user's personal data. The announcement lists US states including California, Colorado, New Jersey and Connecticut as places where GPC already has legal effect.

The Safari version is a free install from the Mac App Store, with EFF as the seller. The announcement warns that installing an extension in Safari takes more steps than in other browsers, and links to Apple's instructions. This is the first release of the Safari version, and problems can be reported by email to extension-devs@eff.org or on GitHub.

Perspective

According to privacybadger.org, Privacy Badger identifies trackers algorithmically, whereas most blocking tools rely on manually maintained lists of domains. It watches whether third-party domains use cookies that can uniquely identify a browser, "supercookies" kept in local storage, and canvas fingerprinting (identifying a device from subtle differences in how its browser draws graphics). A third-party domain caught tracking the user on three different websites gets blocked. Ads that do not track the user are left alone.

Privacy Badger uses lists as well. By default it regularly pulls in data from Badger Sett, EFF's training project, on the trackers Badger Sett has found across thousands of popular websites. A separate yellowlist holds third-party domains that websites need in order to work, and for these Privacy Badger loads the content and blocks only third-party cookies and the referrer. On the same site, the yellowlist is described as a compromise for usability that EFF hopes to do without in the long run.

According to Apple's support page, Safari deletes cookies and website data from third-party sites the user has not visited and interacted with directly. Safari also presents websites with a simplified version of the system configuration, so that every Mac looks more alike and trackers find it harder to identify a device. According to EFF's announcement, Privacy Badger is effective on its own. Used alongside an ad blocker, or with the tracking protection in Safari's Advanced settings applied to all windows, it can also block trackers that are missing from other tools' lists or that those tools choose not to block.

According to privacybadger.org, GPC is meant to be a legally binding request to every company wherever an applicable privacy law exists. The states listed in the announcement are all in the US, and our inference is that websites elsewhere may ignore the signal. According to the same site, Privacy Badger also sends the Do Not Track signal (a browser signal asking websites not to track the user). A domain is blocked only if it keeps collecting unique identifiers after receiving both signals.

During installation, the browser warns that the extension can access data on all websites, and according to privacybadger.org, browsing data is not shared unless the user submits a broken-site report. The privacy label on the Mac App Store page reads "Data Not Collected", information provided by the developer that Apple has not verified. Freedom of the Press Foundation, a press freedom organisation, also reminded readers in its introduction to the Safari version to install only extensions they trust. Beyond permissions, a website may stop working properly, and according to EFF's announcement, Privacy Badger can then be disabled for that site alone.

Among the Asian rules on ad tracking that we, a community based in Taiwan, have collected, Article 20 of Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act requires a non-government entity using personal data for marketing to stop once the person refuses, and to offer a way to refuse the first time it markets to them. Article 24 of mainland China's Personal Information Protection Law requires anyone pushing information or commercial marketing to individuals through automated decision-making to also offer an option that does not target their personal characteristics, or a convenient way to refuse. Japan's amended Telecommunications Business Act, in force since 16 June 2023, requires online information services such as messaging, social media, search and news to give notice of or publish the user data they send to outside parties through tags or modules, or else obtain consent or offer a way to opt out. None of these provisions mentions GPC or Do Not Track, and we have not checked whether regulators in these places treat either signal as a refusal or an opt-out.

An iTunes lookup API query on 8 November returned the app in the Mac App Store storefronts for mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Japan and South Korea, free in each and at the same version, 2026.10.22, though we did not open those storefronts with local accounts. The listing's 28 languages include Japanese and Chinese but not Korean. In mainland China, GreatFire rated www.eff.org as unreliable, with interference in 23% of the last 61 conclusive tests up to its latest test on 12 October. privacybadger.org was reachable from mainland China at GreatFire's last test on 31 May, and has not been tested since.

If you use Safari on a Mac and want less cross-site tracking, first make sure Safari is at 26.5 or later and the system at macOS 15.7.7 or later, then install the extension from the Mac App Store and enable it in Safari following Apple's instructions. The extension's interface is available in Traditional Chinese, though as of 8 November privacybadger.org has no Traditional Chinese version. Privacy Badger blocks third-party trackers, and data collected by the sites you visit directly is outside its scope (when you visit YouTube directly, for example, neither YouTube's own tracking nor its ads are blocked). As of 8 November, there is no version for browsing on iPhone and iPad.

item.title: US border device search figures and the unlock decision before travel
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: According to FPF on 4 November, citing data obtained by CBC News, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) searched 32% more travellers' electronic devices in the first three quarters of fiscal year 2026 than in the same period a year earlier. The searches affect travellers entering and leaving the US, and non-US citizens who refuse to unlock a device may be refused entry. People carrying source material to the US need to decide before departure whether they will unlock if asked.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 12 sources, including U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Freedom of the Press Foundation, CBP

On 4 November, the Freedom of the Press Foundation (FPF), a US press freedom organisation, cited data obtained by Canada's CBC News in its digital security newsletter: in the first three quarters of fiscal year 2026, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) searched 32% more travellers' electronic devices than in the same period a year earlier. The US federal fiscal year begins in October of the previous calendar year, so those three quarters run from October 2025 to June 2026. Both US citizens and foreign visitors entering or leaving the US can be searched, but the consequences of refusing to unlock a device differ. In FPF's words, border searches "affect a very small percentage of international travelers, but they are disproportionately travelers who are not U.S. citizens."

As relayed by FPF, the CBC report counts 47,517 basic searches in those three quarters and another 4,564 advanced searches. The report also notes that CBP will not reveal how many of the searches took place at the northern border with Canada or the southern border with Mexico, and FPF, citing it, writes that the agency "is reportedly on track for a record-setting year for device searches." Adding up the quarterly table on CBP's website, we count 52,081 searches in the first three quarters, already more than 90% of the 55,318 for the whole of fiscal year 2025. CBP's page notes that the statistics may change when finalised, and as of 8 November the table had no figure for the fourth quarter.

The difference between the two kinds of search is set out in CBP Directive 3340-049B, an internal directive that took effect on 1 January and replaced the earlier 049A. It defines an advanced search as "any search in which an officer connects equipment, wired or wireless, to copy and/or analyze the contents of an electronic device," allowed only with reasonable suspicion that the traveller has broken a law CBP enforces, or a national security concern, and with supervisory approval. Connecting equipment merely to bypass a password, overcome encryption or translate content does not count as an advanced search. Every other search is a basic search, which an officer may conduct "with or without suspicion," and which the journalist checklist written by FPF with EFF (the Electronic Frontier Foundation) describes as manually looking through information on a device.

The same directive obliges travellers to present devices "in a condition that allows inspection of the device and its contents." If a device is protected by a passcode or encryption, officers may ask for the traveller's assistance or for the passcode, and a recorded passcode is not to be uploaded into CBP systems. A device that cannot be inspected may be detained, ordinarily for no more than five days, with longer detention needing higher-level approval. Copies of a device's contents are kept for at most 21 days after the search ends, except in cases such as probable cause to suspect a violation.

Under the directive, officers may not intentionally use a device to reach information stored only in the cloud, so during a search they ask the traveller to turn on airplane mode and turn off Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, or cut the connection themselves. For material covered by attorney-client privilege, the directive sets out a procedure of contacting the legal office and forming a separate filter team. Work-related information carried by journalists is grouped with medical records as other possibly sensitive information, which "shall be handled in accordance with any applicable federal law and CBP policy."

The body of the directive does not distinguish between US citizens and foreign travellers in what follows a refusal to provide a passcode. According to CBP's explanatory page, whether a device can be inspected does not by itself decide admission, and a US citizen will not be refused entry on that ground alone. The same page says a citizen's device may still be detained and clearance may take longer, while for foreign travellers the matter can be weighed in the admission decision. FPF's article puts the possible detention at days or weeks and the checklist at days to months, and the checklist warns that refusing may bring scrutiny of a green card holder's permanent resident status, and that foreign nationals arriving on a visa or under the visa waiver programme may be denied entry.

Perspective

The US Supreme Court has not yet ruled on border searches of phones, and the federal courts of appeals differ depending on how the search is done. EFF's July article reports that the Fourth Circuit held manual searches to be routine, needing neither a warrant nor individualised suspicion. On 18 September the legal blog Volokh Conspiracy summarised a Second Circuit ruling from the day before, which likewise held that a manual search of a phone needs no warrant and no suspicion at all; the traveller in that case was a lawful permanent resident of the US. We have not read either ruling in full.

According to a 13 October overview by the law firm Holland & Knight, the circuits are further apart on forensic searches, with the Fourth and Ninth Circuits requiring reasonable suspicion. The Eleventh Circuit holds that none is needed, and the remaining circuits have either left the question open or not yet faced it. The overview's authors expect the Supreme Court to take up the issue before long. CBP's directive also provides that where binding circuit precedent imposes different requirements, the place where the search begins determines which rules apply.

CBP's directive presents border searches as part of carrying out its customs, immigration, law enforcement and homeland security responsibilities, used among other things to detect terrorism, smuggling and child sexual abuse material. It states that "courts have rejected a categorical exception to the border search doctrine for electronic devices" (the doctrine under which border searches generally need no warrant), and that some of its own requirements are imposed "as a policy matter," "above and beyond prevailing constitutional and legal requirements." On its border searches page, EFF argues that "a warrant based on probable cause, issued by a judge, is required for border device searches." In the Second Circuit case, one judge wrote a concurrence (agreeing with the outcome while giving separate reasons) arguing for at least some suspicion, and the author of the Volokh Conspiracy post argues that a warrant should be required.

FPF's article notes that makers of forensic tools rely on exploit research that can take months, "so simply keeping your device up to date will make it significantly harder for someone to make a forensic copy of your device." It also recommends a long, unique passcode and powering the device down before going through border security, which returns it to its encrypted state and significantly reduces what forensic tools can extract. Modern phones encrypt the disk by default, while computer users should check that FileVault on a Mac or BitLocker on Windows is turned on. The directive treats connecting equipment to bypass a passcode as a basic search, needing neither reasonable suspicion nor supervisory approval, and FPF's article does not discuss whether updates and powering down still help in that situation.

The checklist advises deciding before the trip whether to unlock a device or give the passcode if asked. It puts the chance of being selected for a device search at less than 0.01% of international travellers, but adds that depending on what information you carry, "the impact of a search may be quite high." For those who plan to unlock, it suggests moving files, chat histories and contacts they do not want seen off the device beforehand, emptying the trash, and temporarily leaving groups on messaging apps such as Signal. It also suggests logging out, on the day of travel, of accounts that border officials should not be able to access.

People who will carry source material into or out of the US can read the checklist before they leave, and FPF and EFF each host a copy in English. The checklist also recommends noting down a lawyer familiar with border cases and telling family or friends when you expect to clear the border. EFF's Surveillance Self-Defense site has a page of border advice as well, last reviewed in October 2018, which warns that some of its recommendations may be out of date. The checklist was published in June 2025, before the new directive took effect in January, but its descriptions of basic and advanced searches match the new directive's definitions.

We, a community based in Taiwan, also looked at device inspection at borders in parts of Asia. In mainland China, the Ministry of State Security issued two sets of procedural rules for state security organs, one for administrative enforcement and one for criminal cases, which took effect on 1 July 2024; we did not obtain their text, only the account state security officers gave China News Service, a state news agency, on 11 June 2024. According to that report, officers may inspect electronic devices only while carrying out counter-espionage work and only those of individuals and organisations connected with it, which the officers said rules out ordinary inbound travellers. Each inspection needs approval from the head of a state security organ at the level of a city divided into districts or above, even in an emergency, and the officer must show enforcement credentials with the person inspected or a witness present.

For Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan, as of 8 November we found no published rule or official guidance on customs examining the contents of travellers' phones or other devices. Article 105 of Japan's Customs Act lets customs officers question people and inspect goods and the related books and documents, including electromagnetic records, but we found no provision in the Act that expressly covers devices carried by travellers and did not determine whether Article 105 extends to them.

When comparing practices across places, on privacy one can ask whether a search needs suspicion or a warrant, how long copies of device contents are kept, and whether journalists' material has its own handling procedure. On effectiveness, one can ask whether raising the threshold for searches would affect CBP's work on smuggling and national security cases. Since CBP does not disclose how searches are spread across its borders, one can also ask whether outsiders can judge from the published figures whether searches are being used for the purposes the directive lists.

item.title: Known flaws exploited on older iOS and Android, and a claimed Lockdown Mode bypass
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Security firm Sekoia on 4 November published details of a campaign that attacked phones through websites. According to its report, every flaw used had already been patched, and phones updated to the latest system are not affected. Separately, the research team Calif posted a video on 3 November claiming to bypass Lockdown Mode on an iPhone; as of 8 November there were no technical details and no response from Apple.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 32 sources, including Sekoia, Apple, Google Chrome Releases

Security firm Sekoia published an investigation on 4 November into a watering-hole attack, in which attackers compromise websites their targets are likely to visit and wait for them to arrive. Code planted on the sites served each visitor an exploit matched to their phone's operating system and browser version. Both iPhones and Android phones were in scope, with the Android side aimed at older versions of Chrome and a Qualcomm chip driver. According to Sekoia's report, every flaw used had already been patched, and phones updated to the latest system are not affected.

In an unrelated development, the research team Calif posted a video on 3 November claiming to have run an exploit on an iPhone 18 Pro with Lockdown Mode turned on (Apple's hardened protection for a small number of high-risk users). The accompanying post, as reproduced by Privacy Guides and MacRumors, read: "Lockdown Mode helps, until it doesn't." As of 8 November Calif had released only the video, with no technical details, and we found no response or fix from Apple.

According to the report, Sekoia found in mid-October 2026 that several high-profile websites in the United States, Ukraine, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria had been compromised or cloned. The attackers used three routes: injecting JavaScript directly into the sites, setting up proxy servers that impersonated the originals, and, between 27 August and 3 September, compromising the tracking code of Plerdy, a Ukrainian web analytics service (a snippet many sites embed to measure visitor behaviour). In the body of the report, this tracking code is described as loaded by thousands of websites, most of them Ukrainian. According to the introduction, the week-long compromise exposed hundreds of legitimate websites, and their visitors, to the exploits.

All three routes end by loading the same script, which profiles the visitor's browser and device, and the server then delivers a matching exploit chain without any action from the user. The report lists three chains, two aimed at iOS 16.7 and iOS 18.5 and one at Chrome for Android versions 139 to 145 (excluding 143). On iPhones the payloads took cookies (data a site stores in the browser to keep you logged in) or full device data, and on Android they took Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords, without remaining installed on the phone. Sekoia assesses that the data collected fits intelligence-gathering goals, and that the attackers may have used the cookies to reuse logged-in sessions and get into services such as webmail.

The report attributes the campaign to APT29 with moderate to high confidence, based on overlaps in technique, operational patterns, victims and infrastructure. According to the report, APT29 is widely attributed to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, while the exploits may have come from a third party. The compromised sites include a Ukrainian energy company, an American trade association, European political parties and Bulgarian military-related sites. When the report was published, it was still unclear whether the attackers were after visitors to particular sites or were trying to collect data from as many unpatched phones as possible.

Apple patched the iOS flaws Sekoia lists between May 2024 and February 2026, the last of them in iOS 26.3. The Chrome flaw was fixed in desktop Chrome 146 in March 2026, and the flaw Sekoia describes in the driver for Qualcomm's Adreno graphics chip appears among the Qualcomm components in the August 2025 Android Security Bulletin.

The chain aimed at iOS 16.7 uses two flaws, and according to Sekoia it should work from iOS 16.0 to 17.4. One of them, CVE-2024-27834, was fixed in iOS 16.7.8 in May 2024. The other, CVE-2025-43529, does not appear on any of the three Apple security content pages for iOS 16.7 that we checked, released between September 2025 and May 2026. The report gives no indication of whether the chain still works once one of the two is patched, so we cannot confirm its statement that "each flaw was resolved by the respective vendor before this campaign began" for this older line.

According to the descriptions of the video by Privacy Guides and MacRumors, the attacker starts the jailbreak (removing iOS restrictions to gain higher privileges) by sending a malicious PDF to the iPhone 18 Pro over AirDrop. The phone is then updated to iOS 27.2, and the jailbreak is still there afterwards. MacRumors adds that the file in the video was accepted by the user, and that it is unclear whether the jailbreak could be installed on a phone already running iOS 27.2. According to MacRumors, Calif had previously said it was disclosing the flaws to Apple and did not plan to release a jailbreak tool for ordinary users.

According to MacTrast's report, videos like this are easy to fake now that AI-generated video is widespread, and the jailbreak may have been in place before recording began. Separately from Calif's video, Apple's reply to TechCrunch on 27 March was that it was not aware of any device with Lockdown Mode enabled being compromised by mercenary spyware. The latest version listed on Apple's security releases page is iOS 27.2, released on 26 October, which predates Calif's video.

Perspective

Sekoia's campaign relied on n-day flaws, meaning flaws the vendor has already disclosed and fixed but that remain on devices that have not been updated, as opposed to zero-days the vendor does not yet know about. Whether an attack succeeds depends on which version the visitor's phone is running. On Apple's security releases page, keeping software up to date is described as one of the most important things you can do for your device's security. According to Google's Android help page, update schedules vary by device, manufacturer and mobile carrier, and older devices can't always run newer Android versions.

On an iPhone, updates are under Settings, General, Software Update, where Automatic Updates can also be turned on so the phone installs updates overnight while charging and connected to Wi-Fi. According to Apple's security releases page, as of 8 November the iPhone 11 and later can update to iOS 27.2. Apple has also released iOS 26.7.2 for an older system line and iOS 18.7.11 for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, all three on 26 October.

According to Google's help page, system updates on an Android phone are in the Settings app under System, Software updates, and the security update date is shown under About phone. Names may differ by manufacturer and interface language. Chrome is updated separately through the Play Store, under Manage apps & device. According to iThome's report, Sekoia urged users to update their operating systems and browsers as soon as possible.

According to Apple's support page, Lockdown Mode is designed for the very few people who, because of who they are or what they do, might be targeted by highly sophisticated attacks, and most people are never targeted in this way. With it on, most message attachments are blocked (certain images, video and audio excepted) and link previews are unavailable. Some websites may load slowly or not work properly, and the iPhone turns off 2G and 3G cellular support. Apple's guidance is to update to the latest software before turning it on, for a complete set of protections.

According to MacRumors' description, the attack in the video begins when the user accepts a PDF sent over AirDrop. From that condition we infer that not accepting AirDrop files from unknown senders avoids the scenario shown in the video. Since Calif has not published details, it is unclear whether other routes could achieve the same result, and Apple's page has no mention of Lockdown Mode restrictions on AirDrop or PDFs.

According to Google's help page, Android has a comparable Advanced Protection setting, which requires a screen lock before it can be turned on. It is under Settings, Security & Privacy, Other settings, Advanced Protection; once Device protection is on, Google Play Protect cannot be turned off, apps from unknown sources are blocked, and Chrome's JavaScript optimizer and WebGPU (an interface that lets web pages use the graphics chip directly) are disabled. The trade-offs are that Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) may slow the phone down and the phone may fail to connect to a cellular network where only 2G coverage is available. Google's page has nothing on whether these features would stop the chains Sekoia lists.

Calif's claim could not be verified as of 8 November, we found no response from Apple, and no update after iOS 27.2 was available to install. The next things to watch are whether Apple releases a fix or responds, and whether Calif publishes technical details. According to Privacy Guides, those details are likely to come only after Apple has released a patch and people have had time to install it.

When we checked on 8 November, we found no alert about Sekoia's campaign or Calif's video from the computer emergency response teams of Taiwan, Hong Kong or Japan. Taiwan's TWCERT/CC (Taiwan Computer Emergency Response Team / Coordination Center) listed CVE-2025-43529 in its weekly digest of the US Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 24 December 2025, and CVE-2026-3910, the Chrome flaw, in the digest published on 19 March 2026. Hong Kong's HKCERT published a routine bulletin on Apple products on 27 October, covering a different flaw from those in this article. We found no entries for these flaws at Japan's JPCERT/CC and its vulnerability database JVN, or at mainland China's CNVD, whose search requires a login or JavaScript and returned nothing, though not finding them does not mean none exist.

For readers in mainland China, Apple's Simplified Chinese Lockdown Mode page, dated 18 September, carries the same description as the English page and mentions no regional restriction. The Chrome update route above runs through the Play Store, which GreatFire's measurements showed as 100% blocked in mainland China as of 1 November, a third-party test of whether the site can be reached. Google's Advanced Protection page lists no regional limits, and we found no official statement on whether it, or Google's update instructions, apply to Android phones sold in mainland China.

Anyone with a phone that has not been updated can check the version in Settings, and according to Sekoia's report, updating blocks the already-patched flaws used in this campaign. iPhone owners can compare against the three versions above, and those still on iOS 16 can update to iOS 16.7.16 (released 11 May 2026), the latest version we found for that line. We derived the Android comparison from the version ranges in the report: a security update date earlier than the August 2025 bulletin, or a Chrome version between 139 and 145, falls within the range the report lists. We could not find the Chrome for Android version that fixed the Chrome flaw.

item.title: Takedown requests on X against Indian accounts that document online censorship
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: Two notices bearing the name of the Delhi Police reached X between late October and early November, asking it to remove or withhold in India the accounts of two digital rights organisations and of an account that documents blocking orders. As of 8 November, the notices had not been officially confirmed as genuine, and we could not find out whether X had complied. Under X's policy, withholding is limited to the country that made the request.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 16 sources, including SFLC.in, Internet Freedom Foundation, Newslaundry

On 31 October and 2 November, two notices bearing the name of the Delhi Police reached X, asking it to remove or withhold (hide content only in specific countries) three accounts that document online censorship. SFLC.in, an Indian digital rights organisation named in the notices, published the copies X forwarded to it and described the notices as "purportedly issued". As of 8 November, neither the Delhi Police nor the Indian government had publicly confirmed them. According to X's help page, withholding is limited to the country that made the request, so what readers outside India see is not affected.

It began on 29 October, when two Indian digital rights organisations and an X account that compiles blocking orders received a legal notice claiming to act for the RSS, a Hindu nationalist organisation, demanding that they stop documenting restricted content. According to Newslaundry, relaying IFF (the Internet Freedom Foundation, an Indian digital rights organisation), several RSS functionaries later questioned on X whether the notice was genuine. The two organisations posted the notice publicly on X on 30 October, and those two posts are what the first police notice targeted, on the grounds that they defamed the RSS.

According to SFLC.in's statement of 5 November, the court order fields in both notices were left blank, and the first cited section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS, India's penal code), which covers defamation. The second notice listed the three accounts in their entirety, cited section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, and stated that lawful notices require action within three hours. Section 79 is the safe harbour provision (the protection that keeps platforms from being liable for what users post), and section 79(3)(b) means a platform that fails to remove content after receiving notice may lose that protection.

X forwarded copies of both notices to the affected organisations on 3 November, and according to IFF the emails did not say whether X had acted on them. Reuters reported on 4 November that both organisations' accounts were still viewable that afternoon, and that X, the Delhi Police, India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the RSS had not responded to its requests for comment. As of 8 November we could find nothing on later developments or responses, nor whether the notices had been submitted to a database of takedown notices such as Lumen.

SFLC.in checked where the notices came from. The IP address of the sending server is registered to the Delhi Police and is listed in the domain's SPF record (a public setting that lists which servers may send mail for a domain), yet emails sent to the two police addresses given in the notices bounced. Since the two findings point in different directions, SFLC.in did not draw a conclusion about authenticity from them. It asked the Delhi Police and X for clarification and, as of 5 November, had received no official reply.

SFLC.in also tested X's Law Enforcement Request form. X's Legal Request Portal sends a verification link to an official email address, but this form did not. On 4 November, using a made-up email address, SFLC.in submitted a request targeting its own post, and X logged it all the same. By that afternoon the form had been changed to send a verification code to the submitted address, and as of 8 November X had not publicly explained the flaw or the fix.

Perspective

Whether a notice is valid depends on the law it cites and on who submitted it, and the people affected can only appeal once they have been notified. Besides notices, India has another route under section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, through which the central government blocks content by an order that records its reasons in writing. According to the Apple notice the developer made public, the removal of Bitchat from the App Store in India on 3 October cited section 69A (see Dispute over the removal of the Bluetooth mesh messaging app Bitchat in India).

Our inference is that a notice combined with a three-hour deadline leaves a platform very little time to judge whether a request is valid. Whether a form verifies the identity of the person submitting it therefore affects whether impersonated requests can enter a platform's handling process. SFLC.in asked X through which channel the two notices had been submitted and, as of 5 November, had no answer.

According to X's help page, X determines a user's country from location information it receives, and withheld posts and accounts carry a notice. One kind of notice means X withheld the content in response to a valid legal demand, such as a court order, and the other means X withheld it under local law in response to a report filed through specific support channels. Both notices in this case are titled Illegal Content Report, so our inference is that if the content were withheld, it would more likely carry the local-law notice. X has not said how it classified these requests.

The same help page says that, unless prevented by something like a sealed court order, X notifies affected people by email to the address registered on the account or in the app. The notification usually includes a copy of the request, and people can appeal by replying to the email where content was withheld on a legal demand, or through the Help Center where it was withheld under local law. We infer from this that an organisation whose registered inbox goes unread may not learn that its account has been withheld, and may not receive the copy of the request. People who run organisation accounts in India can check the registered inbox regularly and, if X notifies them, appeal through the channel given in the notification.

On the defamation offence the notices cite, SFLC.in's analysis is that criminal defamation under the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, so police need a magistrate's order before acting. SFLC.in also argues that the officials the Delhi government authorised in June to issue such notices do not include the post that signed them, and that restricting entire accounts rather than specific content fails the tests of necessity and proportionality (this is the organisation's analysis, not a finding by a court or the government). Reuters added the Indian government's general position, not specific to this case, that its directives to platforms target unlawful or misleading content and respect lawful expression.

According to Inc42 and SFLC.in, relaying a report by the Indian Express, MeitY has begun discussing whether to reconsider safe harbour for social media platforms. As relayed by Inc42, the report says the government is studying whether to limit the protection to internet service providers, telecom operators and peer-to-peer messaging platforms, and that the discussions are still exploratory. SFLC.in relays the reasoning that platforms curate and amplify content with algorithms and so are already publishers. MeitY had made no public statement as of 8 November, and linking the police notices to the safe harbour discussion is our own connection, because both involve section 79.

Citing Supreme Court precedent, SFLC.in argues that section 79 is a statutory protection, not a privilege that executive discretion can withdraw. It also warns that if platforms become liable for user content, political speech, journalism and criticism of officials are the most likely to be over-removed. In September, MediaNama analysed what government sources had said about Meta and concluded that the position then rested entirely on anonymous briefings, and that safe harbour is a defence platforms raise when sued, for a court to decide. That analysis predates the November Indian Express report, but the sources' statements it examined are similar to that report, and placing the two side by side is our own connection.

We compared how takedown requests reach platforms in three other places in Asia. In Hong Kong, Schedule 4 to the Implementation Rules for Article 43 of the National Security Law lets a designated officer, authorised by the Commissioner of Police in national security cases, require a platform to take a disabling action on a message without a magistrate's warrant, and the schedule does not say the publisher must be given reasons or a route of appeal. In Taiwan, Article 46 of the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act requires a platform told by the competent authority that content harms children to restrict children's access or remove the content, with no court procedure, though the provision protects children only. In mainland China, Article 52 of the Cybersecurity Law, as amended in 2025 and in force since 1 January 2026, has the state internet regulator and other authorities order network operators to stop transmission and have content from outside China blocked, and we found no requirement in the laws we read to go to a court first.

Transparency reports are one place where such requests appear. According to Hong Kong Free Press in 2023, citing Google's transparency report, the Hong Kong government asked Google to remove 330 items in 2022, 57 of them related to national security, up from 116 items in 2021. These are 2022 figures, not current ones.

Readers outside India do not need to change any settings. Points to watch next are whether X withholds these accounts in India, whether the Delhi Police or MeitY responds publicly, and whether the safe harbour discussion becomes a formal amendment or draft rules.

In its article of 6 November, EFF called on platforms to be transparent about the requests they receive, to notify affected users, and to provide avenues for appeal against restrictions. When comparing platforms, readers can also look at whether a platform verifies the identity of whoever submits a request and whether notices come with a court order. Since the government, as relayed by Reuters, says its directives target unlawful and misleading content, one question is whether platforms can tell, within the deadline, whether a notice is genuine and lawful. We found no public assessment of whether, once safe harbour is narrowed, platforms would remove unlawful content more precisely or remove more lawful speech.

item.title: Wero payments and Play Integrity checks in the Dutch ASN Bank app
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: According to user reports, ASN Bank's Android app in the Netherlands has, since version 1.36.3 (updated in mid-October), intermittently blocked Wero payments on systems without Google certification such as GrapheneOS, while the app itself still opens and shows accounts. As of 8 November we could find no announcement from ASN. People planning to switch to GrapheneOS can take it as an example of a bank moving a payment feature onto Google's check.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 11 sources, including GitHub, ASN Bank, Android Developers

According to user comments on a GitHub project that tracks banking app compatibility, the Android app of Dutch bank ASN Bank has, since version 1.36.3 was released in mid-October, intermittently blocked Wero payments on systems without Google certification, such as GrapheneOS (a privacy-hardened phone operating system built on the Android Open Source Project). As of 8 November we could find no announcement from ASN, and what is known comes from support and complaint replies that users have posted. The reports so far involve only ASN and SNS Bank, which also belongs to de Volksbank, and one SNS Bank app user wrote that the app still opens and shows accounts but can no longer pay with Wero. Readers outside the Netherlands will not run into this directly, but people planning to switch to GrapheneOS can take it as an example of a bank moving a payment feature onto Google's check.

iDEAL is a common way to pay in Dutch online shops. Security.nl reported in April 2025, citing what Wero's operator EPI (European Payments Initiative) told the Dutch newspaper AD, that Wero is to replace iDEAL completely by the end of 2027. Wero is built into each bank's app and is also available as a standalone app. ASN's help page says iDEAL is gradually becoming Wero from 2026, and online shops will show the name "iDEAL | Wero".

PrivSec's compatibility list names ASN as "ASN Bank (De Volksbank)", and one reporting user described ASN and SNS Bank as the same app under different branding. According to users, the message the app shows when a payment is blocked uses the "iDEAL | Wero" name and says the phone or app installation does not meet the bank's security requirements. On the same version some people paid successfully, and others reported that it worked only some of the time. Reporters describe the old and new payment flows separately: one user wrote that the old iDEAL | Wero flow goes through, while the new Wero flow fails Play Integrity, a Google service that lets apps check the device and system they run on.

According to a reply from ASN's IT support that a user posted, GrapheneOS is not supported for Wero, and the device has to meet Wero's security requirements. Several users posted almost identical replies to their complaints. The reason given in them is that iDEAL | Wero relies on the standard security checks of mainstream operating systems, and alternative systems bypass or replace these built-in protections, so iDEAL | Wero cannot guarantee that transactions are secure. The replies also state that ASN is looking with iDEAL | Wero into whether alternative operating systems could be supported in future, but cannot make any commitment for now.

Users also wrote to EPI. In a reply reposted by one user, EPI describes its current focus as supporting the most widely used mobile banking platforms and devices, and acknowledges that this may exclude people who do not use mobile banking and people who prefer systems and devices outside the Apple and Android ecosystems. As of 8 November we could find no public version of these letters.

Perspective

According to the Android developer documentation, Play Integrity returns verdicts at several levels. Basic integrity (MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY) only requires passing basic system integrity checks; the bootloader (the program that loads the operating system at startup) may be unlocked, and the device need not be certified. Device integrity (MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY) requires the app to run on a "genuine and certified Android device", and from Android 13 also requires hardware-backed proof that the bootloader is locked and that a certified manufacturer image is loaded. GrapheneOS is not mentioned in the documentation, and it is our inference from the device integrity conditions that a system without Google certification cannot obtain that verdict.

GrapheneOS's usage guide states that it passes the basic integrity check but is not certified by Google. GrapheneOS does not intend to work around the check, on the grounds that any workaround would break again whenever the check is improved.

We could find no official information on which level ASN requires. One user running LineageOS (another uncertified Android system) reported passing basic integrity and failing device integrity, with only Wero transfers not working (a single case). According to user reports not confirmed by the banks, the Triodos and N26 apps can make Wero payments on GrapheneOS, and Wero can be set up in bunq.

According to a later reply reposted by a user, EPI explained why it uses Play Integrity. By the letter's account, Android hardware key attestation can verify that a key was generated in a hardware environment kept apart from the main system, such as a TEE or StrongBox, and has never left it, but cannot verify the integrity of the calling app or of the running operating system. Play Integrity combines device, system and app signals in a signed token that EPI's backend server verifies. The conclusion in the letter is that hardware key attestation on its own cannot provide the verification EPI's risk and fraud models require.

GrapheneOS, for its part, argues in its attestation compatibility guide that banks should use the standard Android hardware attestation API and add GrapheneOS's published official signing keys to an allowlist. According to the guide, this API can verify the hardware, firmware, operating system and app, and the key certificates it produces carry the app's ID, signing key fingerprint and version number, along with the fingerprint of the system's verified boot key. In the guide's assessment, hardware attestation is stronger than Play Integrity and does not depend on Google Play services or Google's servers, and Play Integrity's highest level, strong integrity (MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY), is itself built on hardware key attestation. The two sides give different accounts of what the same API can verify, and we have not checked which is correct.

Only one user wrote that the old flow works, and others report that it works only some of the time, so our inference is that it should not be treated as a reliable option. Several users have already complained to ASN and EPI, and GrapheneOS's guide encourages users to write to app developers with a link to the guide.

People planning to switch to GrapheneOS can first check where the banking and payment apps they use stand on PrivSec's compatibility list. The list is built from community reports, GrapheneOS makes no guarantee about its contents, and it includes many banking and payment apps from Taiwan. As of 8 November the ASN entry still carried no note (the list was last updated on 20 October, a day before the first Wero report), so the list may not yet reflect the app update.

GrapheneOS's attestation compatibility guide lists Pixel phones as the supported devices. Google Store's help page, as we checked it on 23 October, lists India, Japan, Singapore and Taiwan as the places in Asia where Pixel phones can be bought from Google Store, and does not include mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau or South Korea; the page covers Google Store only, not other retailers or carriers. In mainland China, GreatFire's Great Firewall measurements have recorded interference with GrapheneOS's update server, releases.grapheneos.org, since 31 January 2026, although only one test in the 90 days before 2 October produced a conclusive result.

PrivSec's list, as updated on 20 October, has sections for Taiwan, Hong Kong, Japan and mainland China, and the only entry among them with a Play Integrity note is one Japanese app, which according to the list cannot be installed from Google Play because of the check. The other entries in those sections carry no Play Integrity note, and the list records what users report about compatibility, not any bank's policy. We could find no public rule on banking apps detecting rooted or uncertified systems from Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority or Japan's Financial Services Agency, and could not obtain the full text of the People's Bank of China's 2019 security standard for mobile financial apps (JR/T 0092-2019) to check whether it contains one. The only Hong Kong statement on rooted devices we found is a single bank's page: DBS Hong Kong suggests that people with a rooted or jailbroken device try a factory reset, or set up its mobile banking app on another device.

We can also infer that keeping a separate Google-certified phone just for payments is another option, and some users mentioned that having a spare phone left them less affected. The cost is one more device to update and look after, and payments on that phone still have to pass Google's check.

item.title: Facial recognition and mall cameras in Hong Kong's SmartView programme
item.dc:creator: anoni.net community
item.description: According to Hong Kong media reports of a police briefing on 5 November, facial recognition is due to be added to the SmartView programme within November, and cameras at the first malls could be connected by the end of the year. The police said the connection complies with Hong Kong's privacy law, but as of 8 November we could find no public response from the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data, and neither facial recognition nor the mall connection had been announced as launched. People who live in Hong Kong or travel there for leisure or business may have their images sent into the police system when they pass through a connected mall, and places outside Hong Kong are not affected.
item.content:encoded:
Based on 19 sources, including Hong Kong Police Force, Hong Kong Free Press, 星島頭條

At a media briefing on 5 November, the Hong Kong Police Force said facial recognition is expected to be added to SmartView within November, and that cameras at the first shopping malls could be connected by the end of the year. SmartView is the police's CCTV network, linking police cameras and cameras of other organisations into one system, and the police also said connecting the malls complies with Hong Kong's privacy law. The police statements are known only through media reports, as we could not find a government press release, and as of 8 November neither facial recognition nor the mall connection had been announced as launched. People who live in Hong Kong or travel there for leisure or business may have their images fed into SmartView when they pass through a connected mall, and places outside Hong Kong are not affected.

As our previous article covered, the Secretary for Security said in an interview on 18 October that CCTV at some malls would be connected to SmartView, and that the public might not need to be told separately. According to Sing Tao Headline, once the cameras are connected, officers can view mall footage from their offices instead of going to the mall in person and completing the paperwork to retrieve it. According to sources cited by HK01, the first four are Olympian City, Tuen Mun Town Plaza, Kwai Chung Shopping Centre and Sierra Life in Fanling. The Collective HK reported that Olympian City and Tuen Mun Town Plaza belong to Sino Group, while Kwai Chung Shopping Centre and Sierra Life belong respectively to the Hong Kong Housing Authority and the Hong Kong Housing Society, two public housing bodies.

Sing Tao Headline, relaying the police explanation, described two ways facial recognition will be used. One is a retrospective search, in which police enter a suspect's facial features into the system and search specified clips, cameras or time periods for whether that person appeared. The other is real-time tracking: for example, after family members provide a recent photo of a high-risk missing elderly person and authorise its use, the system raises an alert as soon as that person appears on camera.

According to Hong Kong Free Press (HKFP), a senior superintendent in the police Operations Bureau said facial recognition would not operate round the clock, and each use would need approval from an officer ranked inspector or above. am730 and Sing Tao Headline quoted the same officer as saying the system can run 24 hours a day to help with searches. Our inference is that the two accounts may refer, respectively, to the system not routinely matching faces across all cameras and to continuous matching once a use is approved. Sing Tao Headline and The Standard also quoted a superintendent in the Operations Bureau as saying that, because of limited computing resources, facial recognition will not be activated on every camera, but resources can be directed to specific cameras for round-the-clock analysis when needed.

On how facial recognition relates to mall cameras, the only explanation we found was in a report by ID Tech. As quoted by ID Tech, a superintendent said the feature can be activated on police cameras and on connected third-party feeds (cameras of malls and other organisations), but will only be triggered when investigating crimes or searching for high-risk missing people.

According to am730 and The Collective HK, during a trial in October the police entered into the system a photo of an elderly person in their eighties who had gone missing after leaving a care home, and found the person within an hour and a half of the report. Figures provided by the police and relayed by am730 show that, as of 31 October, SmartView had helped detect 2,192 criminal cases and arrest 2,831 people.

Footage is generally deleted automatically after about a month: HKFP and Sing Tao Headline say 30 days, while HK01 and ID Tech say no more than 31 days. Sing Tao Headline and The Standard add that this does not apply where keeping the data is in the public interest. Data related to facial recognition is kept longer than footage, up to 180 days according to most reports, some of which attribute the figure to sources. HKFP and The Collective HK describe this data as records such as times and locations, while ID Tech says it also includes photos of faces.

Perspective

According to sources cited by HK01, even after footage has been deleted, the police can use the 180 days of data to establish when and where, and on which camera, a person they searched for appeared. Sing Tao Headline relayed the police reasoning that feature data takes up very little storage, that some criminal cases may have happened six months or a year earlier, and that keeping the data longer improves investigations and cost-effectiveness.

According to HKFP and i-CABLE, the police said that, based on assessments by their legal team and the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD, the statutory body responsible for personal data protection), connecting the malls complies with Hong Kong law. am730 also reported that the police had asked a third-party body to review the arrangement. The PCPD's general CCTV guidance, issued in October 2025 before the briefing, says facial identification and tracking of individuals are not normally expected by the public, so their use must be supported by strong justification. On this connection, i-CABLE quoted an officer as saying the Privacy Commissioner had told the police there was "absolutely no problem, legally or in terms of regulation" (our translation).

According to Sing Tao Headline, the police said their talks with malls had received a very positive response. On 20 October The Collective HK asked the groups that own 16 malls whether they would take part and whether they would put up additional notices; two groups replied that they had no further information, and several, Sino Group among them, did not reply. As of 8 November the police SmartView page still says that notices near third-party cameras are posted at the discretion of the property owner, and HK01 likewise relayed the police as saying there is no requirement and it depends on each mall's practice. Sing Tao Headline relayed the police reasoning that malls already display notices that CCTV is in use, and that after consulting the Department of Justice and the PCPD the police concluded SmartView notices need not be required under every camera, though they would encourage malls to post them.

Sing Tao Headline and The Standard relayed the police position that the system is used only to safeguard national security, prevent and detect crime, and maintain public safety and order, and that officers must pass two internal tests before accessing footage (whether SmartView is essential, and whether the cameras and time periods match the purpose of the investigation). The police also said the cameras capture only public places, and that operating procedures were set based on an independent privacy impact assessment (a review, before launch, of how a system affects personal data) and discussions with the PCPD.

In its report, the Economic Digest added its own comment that specific privacy safeguards, the scope of data use and the oversight mechanism have not yet been disclosed. As of 8 November, the reports do not say whether the 180 days of data covers only the people searched for or everyone who passes a camera, whether the connected mall cameras also capture only public places, or whether data generated by facial recognition can be requested by the people concerned. The PCPD's view is known only through the police account, and we could find no statement from the PCPD or reply to the media (the press release page on the PCPD's website could not be loaded). Nor could we find any public position on the briefing from mall owners, Legislative Council members, academics or civil society groups.

People who neither live in Hong Kong nor plan to travel there do not need to do anything. The police have not said which malls beyond the four named in the media will be connected, and notices depend on whether each mall posts them, so our inference is that people passing through a mall may not be able to tell in advance which cameras feed into SmartView. People caught on camera, including visitors, can use the PCPD's prescribed form to make a data access request to the organisation holding the footage, and requests to the police can be made in person at a police station, by post or online. As our previous article also noted, the police can claim an exemption under section 58 of the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance where giving access would be likely to prejudice the prevention or detection of crime.

We compared rules on facial recognition in three other places in Asia. In mainland China, measures on facial recognition in force since 1 June 2025 require that facial recognition equipment in public places be necessary for public security and marked with a conspicuous notice, though the text does not say whether this applies in practice to systems the police build themselves. In Taiwan, we found no law expressly governing police use of facial recognition in the two laws we searched (the Police Power Exercise Act and the Personal Data Protection Act; other laws were not checked), and Article 10 of the former, which lets police coordinate the installation of CCTV cameras or use existing recording equipment to collect data in public places, says nothing about notices or facial recognition.

In Japan, according to government answers in the Diet in 2021, police in individual cases obtain suspects' face images from security cameras under the Code of Criminal Procedure, with the cooperation of the cameras' managers, and compare them with suspect photos the police hold. For private businesses, a FAQ from Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission says operators of face-identification camera systems in shops, stations or airports must make clear that facial identification is being used, because the cameras' appearance does not reveal it. The same FAQ recommends posting notices at entrances or camera locations naming the operator, the purpose and a contact, a rule for businesses that does not cover the Japanese police. In Hong Kong, according to the police, SmartView notices at connected malls are left to each mall.

Readers can weigh the programme with a few questions. First, on figures for effectiveness and safeguards, whether the police will publish how often facial recognition is used, how many people are found and cases solved, and how many applications are refused. Second, on oversight, whether any body outside the police force reviews the usage records beyond the inspector's approval and the internal tests. Third, on notices, whether connected malls let passers-by know their images go to the police.

Next, it is worth watching for an announcement that facial recognition has formally launched, the timing and list of the first connected malls, and whether the PCPD responds publicly.
